template.tagline: Same rocket, but the booster flies home.

template.tagline: Dense fuel down low, hydrogen up high.
template.brief: A kerosene first stage does the heavy lifting through the thick air, where dense propellant keeps tanks small. Above it, a wide, light hydrogen stage with two expander engines uses its high specific impulse (about 465 s) to push a 4 t satellite toward geostationary transfer orbit.

benchmark.class: Kerolox or solid booster with a hydrogen upper stage

template.tagline: Clean-burning methane and a booster built to fly again.
template.brief: Five full-flow methane engines on a stainless-steel booster that keeps 40 t of propellant to land. Methane burns cleanly (little soot to clean out between flights) and steel is cheap and tough, at the cost of heavier tanks.

There is nothing to stage.

benchmark.class: Kerolox or solid booster with a hydrogen upper stage
benchmark.text: Hydrogen/oxygen upper stages have flown since the 1960s because their efficiency pays off most where every kilogram of stage mass must be pushed to orbital speed. Their low density makes tanks large, which is why they are rarely used alone on first stages.

sources.claim: first liquid hydrogen upper stage (TODO-review: link)

sources.claim: expander-cycle hydrolox upper-stage engine, vacuum Isp ~450–465 s (TODO-review)

review: Seven kerosene engines on stage 1 (not nine): with nine, thrust over mass reached 21.8 g at stage-1 burnout and the stack broke up. Seven give liftoff TWR about 1.3 and about 17 g at burnout. The upper stage is unthrottled in the sim (about 11 g at burnout); real stages throttle or shut down early.

template.tagline: Clean-burning methane and a booster built to fly again.
template.brief: Five full-flow methane engines on a stainless-steel booster that keeps 40 t of propellant to land. Methane burns cleanly (little soot to clean out between flights) and steel is cheap and tough, at the cost of heavier tanks.

benchmark.class: Reusable methalox medium launcher
benchmark.text: In the 2020s several launch companies moved to liquid methane for reusable boosters, because it leaves little soot inside engines, is denser than hydrogen and easier to store. Many of these vehicles are still in development, so performance numbers are not settled.
